QUESTION OF THE WEEK - A combination of factors has seen the market lower the odds on a fourth rate cut in Australia to 30 percent, after being an even money bet just two weeks ago.
Rate cut expectations began to be wound back after fourth quarter wages data came in at the top end of expectations.

Last week, news of stronger than expected employment growth in January, and RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane's view that some of the effects of the three rate cuts in 1996 were yet to come through, and that the RBA was waiting on the 'living wage' case have unwound expectations back further.

As well, the fact that some of the major commercial banks have cut mortgage rates last week without an RBA cut means that consumers have had a de-facto policy easing, giving the RBA more time to consider its options.
Tuesday's quarterly RBA bulletin article on the economy is expected to confirm the RBA's "wait and see" approach.
Imports Profits* of another cut ABN

IMPORTS - Imports are expected to be helped by seasonal adjustment factors and some growth in capital goods. Capital goods have had some large monthly movements in the second half of 1996, and the December level was over 14 percent below their
June level, and essentially flat with July, which were the lowest since late 1994.

Yet while capital imports have been flat in the second half of 1996, total imports have risen in each of the last six months, with both consumption and intermediate goods imports up. One factor that could see the risk to the low side of forecasts is the fall of the Australian dollar since the last rate cut in December 11.

COMPANY PROFITS - The flat median forecast is based in differing perceptions of how companies were fairing into the end of 1996. Those on the weaker side point to soft activity in the fourth quarter, especially on the retail side, while those on the stronger side say that while retail may have been weak in the quarter, it was not universal weakness across the economy. The company profits data is a partial indicator of GDP and not normally a market mover, but a particularly weak result pointing to low or negative GDP could offer some hope to those holding out for a rate cut, analysts said.
